\chapter{Comer Es Bueno --- The Infinitive as Subject}
\label{ch:comer-es-bueno}
\hlchaptermodality{264}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name an activity and say something about it.}

I can name an activity and say something about it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comer es bueno]{comer es bueno — the infinitive as the subject}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-comer-es-bueno}



\begin{quote}
\emph{El libro es grande.} A noun, then \emph{es}, then what it is.

Now put an \textbf{action} in the noun's place.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the infinitive stands there}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{Comer}} \emph{es bueno.} — Eating is good. \emph{\textbf{Hablar}} \emph{español es bueno.} — Speaking Spanish is good.
\end{quote}

The infinitive — the plain dictionary form — simply occupies the subject slot, and the sentence carries on as normal. Nothing is added and nothing changes shape.

Note the verb after it: \emph{\textbf{es}}, singular. An action counts as one thing, however many words are wrapped around it.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
Here is the trap, and it is entirely an English one.

English uses \emph{-ing} for this — \emph{eating is good} — and you have an \emph{-ing} form now. So it is tempting to reach for \emph{\textbf{comiendo}}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Comiendo es bueno.} — \textbf{wrong.}
\end{quote}

The gerund never does this job in Spanish. It is for an action \textbf{underway}, leaning on \emph{estar}; it is not a name for the activity. The infinitive is the name.

So the two languages divide the work differently, and Spanish's division is the simpler one: English argues about \emph{to eat} against \emph{eating}, and Spanish uses one form for both.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Comer es bueno}
  \item \emph{Hablar español es bueno}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form names an activity — the infinitive or the gerund? (The \textbf{infinitive}.)

And what is the gerund for? (An action \textbf{underway}, with \emph{estar}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(review)]{Review — what happens where two words touch}

\label{lesson:ES-C67-repaso-cuando-dos-palabras-se-tocan}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}One book.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{Un libro}.) \textquotedblleft{}The first book.\textquotedblright{} (\emph{El primer libro}.) Neither word is whole.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{One: the word bites itself short.}

\emph{Uno} $\to$ \emph{un libro}. \emph{Primero} $\to$ \emph{primer libro}. \emph{Mucho} $\to$ \emph{muy}. \emph{Malo} $\to$ \emph{mal}.

And the biting has a condition: it happens \textbf{in front of the noun} and nowhere else. Say \emph{el libro primero} and the \emph{o} comes straight back. That position is also where an ordinal lives in the first place — \emph{el primer libro}, not \emph{el libro primer}.

Your scale of degree is built out of exactly this. \emph{Poco}, \emph{\textbf{bastante}}, \emph{muy} — and the top of it, \emph{muy}, is \emph{mucho} with the end chewed off.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{Two: the two words fuse.}

\begin{quote}
\emph{a + el} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{al}}.  ·  \emph{de + el} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{del}}.
\end{quote}

And then the list stops. Two obligatory contractions, no others — a rare thing to be able to say about any grammar.

\textbf{Three: the word changes shape to stay audible.} \emph{O} is a single letter, and in front of a word starting with \emph{o-} a single letter would vanish. So it becomes \emph{u}: \emph{siete \textbf{u} ocho}.

And the one that went furthest. Latin put \emph{cum} on the \textbf{end} of the pronoun — \emph{mēcum}, \textquotedblleft{}with me.\textquotedblright{} Spanish stopped hearing that ending as a word and put \emph{\textbf{con}} back on the front. \textbf{Conmigo} therefore says \emph{with} twice, and it has been getting away with it for a thousand years.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{uno} $\to$ \emph{un libro}, \emph{primero} $\to$ \emph{primer libro}, \emph{mucho} $\to$ \emph{muy}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many obligatory contractions does Spanish have? (\textbf{Two} — \emph{al}, \emph{del}.) Where does \emph{primero} lose its \emph{o}? (\textbf{In front of} a masculine noun.) And what does \emph{conmigo} say twice? (\emph{\textbf{With}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
